questions.stem: A 49 year old woman has 2 weeks of yellow eyes, poor appetite and aching under her right ribs. She has drunk a bottle of wine a day for 15 years and more since her divorce. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. She is jaundiced with a tender, smooth liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Jaundice, fever and tender hepatomegaly after heavy drinking, with AST more than twice ALT and a mildly raised ALP, is alcoholic hepatitis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: bottle of wine a day for 15 years
steps.x: Heavy drinking, **jaundice, fever, tender hepatomegaly**, and an **AST:ALT ratio over 2**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Alcoholic hepatitis.

elim: Needs biliary obstruction with dilated ducts; the AST:ALT pattern is hepatocellular.
ALT usually exceeds AST, often with high IgG, in a woman without alcohol excess.
Very high ALT in the thousands, with ALT greater than AST.
Transaminases rise into the thousands within 1 to 3 days.

steps.x: **B. Alcoholic hepatitis.** Jaundice + fever + tender liver + AST:ALT ≥2 in a drinker = alcoholic hepatitis.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has spider naevi and palmar erythema. He has been stable for a year, but after a month of heavy drinking he has deepening jaundice, a tender liver, fever and new abdominal swelling with shifting dullness. His temperature is 38.0°C. A diagnostic tap shows 60 neutrophils/mm³. His AST is 210 IU/L and ALT 80 IU/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his decompensation?
questions.e: A binge on a background of cirrhosis causing jaundice, fever, tender liver and new ascites is alcoholic hepatitis precipitating decompensation. A normal ascitic neutrophil count excludes SBP.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: new abdominal swelling with shifting dullness
steps.x: Chronic liver disease signs plus a **binge**, then **jaundice, fever, ascites**; the tap is clean.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Alcoholic hepatitis.

elim: Gives weight loss and a liver mass with raised AFP, not a fever with AST:ALT >2 after a binge.
Causes sudden ascites and pain but not fever with a hepatitic AST:ALT pattern.
Cholestatic, with raised ALP and itch in middle-aged women.
Needs an ascitic neutrophil count above 250/mm³; his is 60.

steps.x: **A. Alcoholic hepatitis.** Alcoholic hepatitis often tips stable cirrhosis into decompensation.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has 10 days of jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. He drinks 12 cans of strong lager a day. His temperature is 37.9°C and pulse rate 98 bpm. He has a tender enlarged liver and mild ankle oedema. Viral hepatitis serology is negative and ultrasound shows no biliary dilatation. Further liver blood tests are taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional blood result?
questions.e: Alcoholic hepatitis raises GGT and lowers albumin, with a raised INR marking severity.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: 12 cans of strong lager a day
steps.x: Heavy drinker with acute hepatitis and **oedema**: what does alcohol do to the liver enzymes?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Raised gamma-glutamyl transferase.

elim: Alcohol gives AST higher than ALT, usually 2:1 or more.
Albumin is low with hepatocellular injury and poor nutrition.
GGT is induced by alcohol and raised.
PT and INR are prolonged as synthetic function fails.

steps.x: **D. Raised gamma-glutamyl transferase.** Alcoholic hepatitis: raised GGT, low albumin, raised INR, AST:ALT ≥2.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department by his wife. He drinks a litre of vodka a day and has been yellow for a week. Today he is drowsy, muddled about the date and has a flapping tremor of the outstretched hands. His temperature is 37.8°C. His capillary glucose is 6.2 mmol/L. His eye movements are full and there is no nystagmus.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his confusion?
questions.e: Alcohol history with jaundice and confusion is alcoholic hepatitis with encephalopathy, a medical emergency; asterixis supports hepatic encephalopathy.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
**Alcohol + jaundice + confusion + asterixis**, normal glucose and eye movements.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hepatic encephalopathy from alcoholic hepatitis.

elim: Gives tremor, sweating and agitation 1 to 3 days after stopping, not jaundice with asterixis.
His capillary glucose is normal.
Possible in drinkers, but flapping tremor with jaundice points to liver failure.
Needs ataxia and ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus; his eye movements are normal.

steps.x: **B. Hepatic encephalopathy from alcoholic hepatitis.** Jaundice + confusion in a drinker = alcoholic hepatitis with encephalopathy: an emergency.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man was treated for alcoholic hepatitis 3 months ago. During admission he became confused and unsteady with abnormal eye movements, which improved after treatment. He now has abstained from alcohol. He is alert, but cannot remember events from earlier in the day and gives detailed, false accounts of where he has been. His liver function is improving.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Alcoholic hepatitis is associated with Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome from thiamine deficiency; persistent anterograde amnesia with confabulation after Wernicke's is Korsakoff syndrome.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: confused and unsteady with abnormal eye movements
cannot remember events from earlier in the day
steps.x: Earlier **Wernicke's** episode, now **amnesia with confabulation** while alert.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Korsakoff syndrome.

elim: Gradual decline in an older person, without preceding Wernicke's.
Causes fluctuating drowsiness with asterixis; he is alert and liver tests are improving.
Gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and dementia.
The acute triad has resolved; this is the chronic amnesic stage.

steps.x: **C. Korsakoff syndrome.** Thiamine deficiency: Wernicke's (acute, reversible) then Korsakoff (amnesia, confabulation).

questions.stem: A 58 year old man is admitted with alcoholic hepatitis. He mentions that for 2 years he has been unable to lay his hands flat on the table. There is a thickened cord in both palms. The doctor tries to straighten his fingers.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his hands?
o: Bony swellings of the distal interphalangeal joints
Finger locks in flexion then clicks straight
Fixed flexion of the ring and little fingers that cannot be corrected passively
questions.e: Dupuytren's contracture, linked with alcohol, causes fixed flexion of the 4th and 5th digits that cannot be corrected passively, often on both sides.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: unable to lay his hands flat
steps.x: A **palmar cord** on **both sides** in a heavy drinker.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fixed flexion of the ring and little fingers that cannot be corrected passively.

elim: Heberden's nodes of osteoarthritis.
Trigger finger, a tendon sheath problem that corrects.
Koilonychia of iron deficiency.
Rheumatoid arthritis.

steps.x: **C. Fixed flexion of the ring and little fingers that cannot be corrected passively.** Dupuytren's: bilateral fixed flexion of ring/little fingers, uncorrectable passively.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman with heavy alcohol use is admitted with 1 week of jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. Her temperature is 38.3°C and pulse rate 100 bpm. She has a tender enlarged liver and no ascites. Chest X-ray, urine and blood cultures are clear. Liver ultrasound shows a large bright liver with no abscess or duct dilatation. Her neutrophils are 13.1 ×10⁹/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her fever?
questions.e: Alcoholic hepatitis itself commonly causes fever and a neutrophilia; once infection is screened for and imaging is clear, the hepatitis explains the fever.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: Chest X-ray, urine and blood cultures are clear
steps.x: Fever and **neutrophilia** with a tender liver, **negative infection screen** and clear ultrasound.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Alcoholic hepatitis.

elim: Needs a dilated biliary tree, absent on ultrasound.
No travel history; jaundice with tender hepatomegaly fits the liver itself.
Ultrasound shows no abscess.
Needs ascites, which she does not have.

steps.x: **B. Alcoholic hepatitis.** Fever and raised WBC are part of alcoholic hepatitis; still screen for infection first.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man has 2 weeks of jaundice, dark urine and fatigue. He drinks 100 units of alcohol a week. His temperature is 37.8°C. His liver is enlarged and tender. Investigations show AST 188 IU/L (<40), ALT 72 IU/L (<40), ALP 160 IU/L (30–130) and bilirubin 145 µmol/L (<21). Liver ultrasound shows hepatomegaly with no gallstones or biliary dilatation.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Tender hepatomegaly with jaundice, AST:ALT above 2, mildly raised ALP and a normal biliary tree in a heavy drinker is alcoholic hepatitis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
AST:ALT about **2.6**, ALP only mildly raised, **no obstruction**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Alcoholic hepatitis.

elim: Gives ALT in the thousands with ALT higher than AST.
Would dilate the common bile duct and give a cholestatic picture.
Mild unconjugated bilirubin rise with normal enzymes and no tender liver.
Painless obstructive jaundice with a dilated duct and very high ALP.

steps.x: **B. Alcoholic hepatitis.** Hepatocellular pattern + AST:ALT >2 + alcohol = alcoholic hepatitis.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man who drinks heavily attends with 1 week of jaundice, fever and right upper quadrant pain. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. He has spider naevi on his chest. The doctor palpates his abdomen.

visual.title: Where the pain is
visual.caption: Right upper quadrant pain over an enlarged liver.

questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal examination?
o: Small, impalpable liver with no tenderness
questions.e: Alcoholic hepatitis gives a tender enlarged liver; a shrunken liver is end-stage cirrhosis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: jaundice, fever and right upper quadrant pain
steps.x: Acute inflammation of the liver in a drinker makes it **swollen and tender**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Tender hepatomegaly.

elim: A palpable non-tender gallbladder with painless jaundice suggests pancreatic cancer.
Flank bruising of severe pancreatitis.
Abdominal aortic aneurysm.
Seen in end-stage cirrhosis, not acute alcoholic hepatitis.

steps.x: **E. Tender hepatomegaly.** Alcoholic hepatitis: jaundice, fever, RUQ pain, tender hepatomegaly.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman is admitted with alcoholic hepatitis. She drinks 2 bottles of wine a day and eats very little. She has jaundice, a tender liver and ankle swelling. Her temperature is 37.6°C and BP 110/68 mmHg. She bruises easily. A clotting screen and serum albumin are sent.
questions.q: Which pair of results is most likely?
questions.e: Alcoholic hepatitis lowers albumin and raises the INR, which is a marker of severity.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
**Oedema** and **easy bruising**: the liver is not making proteins.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Low albumin and raised INR.

elim: Synthetic function is impaired, not preserved.
Albumin falls with poor synthesis and nutrition.
Clotting factor production falls, so INR rises.
Oedema and easy bruising point to impaired synthesis.

steps.x: **D. Low albumin and raised INR.** Alcoholic hepatitis: low albumin, raised INR (severity marker).

questions.stem: A 55 year old man with alcoholic hepatitis has been in hospital for 4 days. He is jaundiced with a tender liver. Over 2 days his abdomen has become more distended and his ankles are swollen. There is shifting dullness. His temperature is 37.5°C. An ascitic tap shows 90 neutrophils/mm³ and his albumin is 26 g/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his abdominal swelling?
o: Ascites from worsening portal hypertension and low albumin
questions.e: Alcoholic hepatitis can worsen portal hypertension causing ascites, made worse by hypoalbuminaemia; a neutrophil count under 250 excludes SBP.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
**Shifting dullness**, clean tap, **low albumin** in active alcoholic hepatitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ascites from worsening portal hypertension and low albumin.

elim: Would cause colicky pain, vomiting and absolute constipation with a tympanic abdomen.
Gives low-gradient ascites with weight loss, not ascites developing during acute alcoholic hepatitis.
Would not give shifting dullness.
Ascitic neutrophils below 250/mm³ exclude it.

steps.x: **A. Ascites from worsening portal hypertension and low albumin.** Alcoholic hepatitis can worsen portal hypertension and cause ascites.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with jaundice, fever and a tender liver admits drinking 80 units a week for 20 years. His AST is 198 IU/L and ALT 76 IU/L. Viral screen and ultrasound exclude other causes. The junior doctor asks whether a test is needed to confirm the diagnosis before treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate basis for confirming the diagnosis?
o: Clinical picture with the liver blood test pattern and alcohol history
questions.e: Alcoholic hepatitis is diagnosed from the clinical picture combined with the LFT pattern (AST:ALT >2, raised bilirubin) and the alcohol history.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.

clues: Viral screen and ultrasound exclude other causes
steps.x: Typical history, **AST:ALT >2**, other causes excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clinical picture with the liver blood test pattern and alcohol history.

elim: Shows structure but cannot diagnose alcoholic hepatitis.
Invasive biliary procedure; there is no obstruction.
Rarely needed when the clinical picture is clear, and risky with coagulopathy.
Shows recent drinking, not liver inflammation.

steps.x: **A. Clinical picture with the liver blood test pattern and alcohol history.** Diagnosis = clinical picture + LFT pattern + alcohol history.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has 2 weeks of jaundice and tender hepatomegaly. She drinks 6 glasses of wine a day but also returned from rural India a month ago and has had unprotected sex with a new partner. Her temperature is 37.7°C. Her AST is 220 IU/L and ALT 105 IU/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to exclude other causes?
questions.e: Alcohol is the likely cause, but travel and sexual risk mean a viral screen is needed to exclude hepatitis A, B, C and E.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.

clues: unprotected sex with a new partner
steps.x: Alcoholic picture, but **travel and sexual exposure** raise viral hepatitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Viral hepatitis screen.

elim: Tests for primary biliary cholangitis, which is cholestatic.
For Wilson's disease, usually in younger patients with neurological signs.
For haemochromatosis, a chronic picture.
Tests for pancreatitis, not hepatitis.

steps.x: **E. Viral hepatitis screen.** First-line bloods include a viral screen to exclude other causes.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man who drinks heavily is found by paramedics confused and sweating at home. He is jaundiced and thin. His pulse rate is 110 bpm, BP 108/66 mmHg and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. He has not eaten for 3 days. His GCS is 13.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: A confused, sweaty, malnourished drinker with liver disease needs a bedside glucose first; hypoglycaemia is quick to find and fix.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Confused, **sweaty**, **not eating**, liver disease: rule out the quickest killer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Capillary blood glucose.

elim: May be needed later, but a reversible metabolic cause must be checked first.
Does not explain acute confusion and can wait.
Not a reliable bedside test and does not change immediate care.
Takes days and does not explain the acute confusion.

steps.x: **A. Capillary blood glucose.** Glucose first in any confused drinker; then thiamine and LFTs.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man is admitted with alcoholic hepatitis. His bilirubin is 290 µmol/L and prothrombin time is 9 seconds above control. He is jaundiced with a tender liver and is alert. His temperature is 37.6°C, he has no GI bleeding and cultures are negative. His Maddrey's discriminant function is calculated (see item resources).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate interpretation of this score?
o: Moderate disease; no change to treatment
Score is invalid without a liver biopsy
Severe disease; urgent liver transplant listing
questions.e: Maddrey's DF = 4.6 × (PT − control) + bilirubin (mg/dL). A score of 32 or more indicates severe disease and prompts consideration of prednisolone.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Score well **above 32**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Severe disease; consider corticosteroids.

elim: A score of 32 or more is severe.
There is no moderate band that ignores steroids above 32.
The score uses only bilirubin and prothrombin time.
Transplant is not first-line in acute alcoholic hepatitis.

steps.x: **D. Severe disease; consider corticosteroids.** MDF ≥32 = severe alcoholic hepatitis: consider steroids.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man is admitted with alcoholic hepatitis. He weighs 54 kg and has lost muscle from his arms and legs. He has agreed to stop drinking. His Maddrey's discriminant function is 22. There is no confusion. A friend has told him he should cut out protein to protect his liver.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate dietary management?
questions.e: Supportive care in alcoholic hepatitis includes stopping alcohol, a high-protein diet and vitamin supplementation.

steps.x: It asks for a management step: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.
**Malnourished** drinker: build him up, do not restrict protein.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: High-protein diet with vitamin supplements.

elim: He is already malnourished.
Protein restriction worsens malnutrition and is not recommended.
Starvation worsens muscle loss and risks hypoglycaemia.
Heavy drinkers are vitamin deficient and need supplementation.

steps.x: **A. High-protein diet with vitamin supplements.** Supportive care: stop alcohol, high-protein diet, vitamins.

questions.stem: A 51 year old man who drinks 2 litres of cider a day is admitted with alcoholic hepatitis. He is jaundiced but alert and orientated, with normal eye movements and gait. His temperature is 37.6°C and BP 122/74 mmHg. His capillary glucose is 5.8 mmol/L. The admitting doctor writes the initial drug chart.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug to give on admission?
questions.e: IV thiamine is given first-line in alcoholic hepatitis to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy, even without neurological signs.

steps.x: It asks for a management step: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.
No neurological signs yet, but he is a heavy drinker: **prevent** Wernicke's.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Intravenous thiamine.

elim: His glucose is normal; glucose without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke's.
For encephalopathy, which he does not have.
Only considered when Maddrey's DF is 32 or more.
For ascites, which he does not have.

steps.x: **B. Intravenous thiamine.** Every admitted heavy drinker: IV thiamine (Pabrinex) to prevent Wernicke's.

questions.stem: A 54 year old man has severe alcoholic hepatitis with a Maddrey's discriminant function of 48. On day 2 he passes black, tarry stool and his haemoglobin falls from 112 to 84 g/L. His pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. His temperature is 37.4°C and cultures are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management regarding corticosteroids?
o: Start prednisolone with a proton pump inhibitor
Steroids are not indicated at this score
Withhold prednisolone while there is active GI bleeding
questions.e: MDF of 32 or more means prednisolone is considered, but only if there are no contraindications such as active infection or GI bleeding.

steps.x: It asks for a management step: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.
Steroid-level severity (**MDF 48**) but **melaena** with a falling Hb.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Withhold prednisolone while there is active GI bleeding.

elim: Still a corticosteroid; the problem is the bleeding, not the route.
Active GI bleeding is a contraindication.
PPI cover does not make steroids safe during an active bleed.
An MDF of 48 is severe; steroids would be considered if not contraindicated.

steps.x: **E. Withhold prednisolone while there is active GI bleeding.** Prednisolone for MDF ≥32 unless active infection or GI bleeding.

questions.stem: A 43 year old woman is admitted with alcoholic hepatitis. She is jaundiced with a tender liver but is alert. Her temperature is 37.5°C. Her Maddrey's discriminant function is 19. She has had IV thiamine and has stopped drinking. The registrar is asked whether to start corticosteroids.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: An MDF below 32 is not severe, so steroids are not indicated; management is abstinence, nutrition and vitamins.

steps.x: It asks for a management step: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.
MDF **below 32**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Supportive care without corticosteroids.

elim: Steroids are only considered when MDF is 32 or more.
Not indicated for non-severe acute alcoholic hepatitis.
Her score of 19 is not severe.
Neither is indicated below the severe threshold.

steps.x: **E. Supportive care without corticosteroids.** MDF <32: supportive care only; ≥32: consider prednisolone.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man is recovering from alcoholic hepatitis. He has abstained for 4 weeks. His abdomen has slowly become distended and there is shifting dullness. His BP is 116/72 mmHg, sodium 134 mmol/L and potassium 4.2 mmol/L. A diagnostic tap shows 40 neutrophils/mm³ and a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 1.6 g/dL.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug treatment?
questions.e: Complications of alcoholic hepatitis are managed as they arise: diuretics, led by spironolactone, for portal-hypertensive ascites.

steps.x: It asks for a management step: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.
Uninfected, **high-gradient** ascites after alcoholic hepatitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Spironolactone.

elim: Not the first-line diuretic for cirrhotic-type ascites.
Thiazides are not used for ascites.
No SBP: neutrophils are under 250/mm³.
ACE inhibitors cause hypotension and renal failure in decompensated liver disease.

steps.x: **E. Spironolactone.** Ascites: diuretics (spironolactone first).

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman with alcoholic hepatitis has become slow and muddled over 2 days. She has a flapping tremor. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. Her glucose is 6.4 mmol/L, there is no bleeding, and infection screen and CT head are normal. She has received IV thiamine.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Complications are managed as they arise: lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy, once other causes such as hypoglycaemia, bleeding and infection are excluded.

steps.x: It asks for a management step: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.

clues: infection screen and CT head are normal
steps.x: **Asterixis** and confusion with other causes excluded: hepatic encephalopathy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Lactulose.

elim: Sedation worsens hepatic encephalopathy and masks deterioration.
Already given, and asterixis points to hepatic, not Wernicke's, encephalopathy.
Benzodiazepines worsen hepatic encephalopathy unless treating withdrawal.
Protein restriction is no longer advised and worsens malnutrition.

steps.x: **C. Lactulose.** Encephalopathy in alcoholic hepatitis: lactulose.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man had severe alcoholic hepatitis 2 years ago and has been abstinent since. He now has end-stage liver disease with refractory ascites, recurrent encephalopathy and a bilirubin of 120 µmol/L despite optimal medical treatment. He is otherwise fit and engaged with alcohol services. His BP is 104/62 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the definitive treatment?
questions.e: Ongoing injury progressed to end-stage disease; with sustained abstinence, liver transplant is the definitive treatment after specialist referral.

steps.x: It asks for a management step: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.
**End-stage** disease, **abstinent**, fit: what fixes the liver itself?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Liver transplant.

elim: Only a 28 day course for severe acute hepatitis; does not reverse end-stage disease.
Controls ascites but is not definitive.
Reduces encephalopathy but does not treat the failing liver.
Treats refractory ascites but worsens encephalopathy and is not definitive.

steps.x: **A. Liver transplant.** End-stage alcohol-related liver disease: refer for liver transplant.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man who drinks 25 units of alcohol a day is admitted with alcoholic hepatitis. Liver biopsy shows ballooned hepatocytes, Mallory-Denk bodies, neutrophil infiltration and fat. The student asks how alcohol damages the liver cells.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of hepatocyte injury?
o: Acetaldehyde and reactive oxygen species from alcohol metabolism
Iron deposition from increased gut absorption
questions.e: Alcohol dehydrogenase and CYP2E1 metabolise alcohol to acetaldehyde and reactive oxygen species, causing direct hepatocyte injury, lipid peroxidation and inflammation.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the stem to the underlying biology.
Injury from **metabolising alcohol** itself.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acetaldehyde and reactive oxygen species from alcohol metabolism.

elim: Autoimmune hepatitis mechanism.
Wilson's disease.
Viral hepatitis; alcohol injures cells directly.
Haemochromatosis.

steps.x: **A. Acetaldehyde and reactive oxygen species from alcohol metabolism.** ADH and CYP2E1 make acetaldehyde + ROS: direct injury, lipid peroxidation, inflammation.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with alcoholic hepatitis has an AST of 260 IU/L and ALT of 95 IU/L. A student already knows that vitamin B6 deficiency reduces ALT synthesis. She asks what else raises the AST in alcohol-related liver injury.
questions.q: Which additional mechanism best explains the high AST?
o: AST release from damaged cardiac muscle
Increased AST synthesis by bile duct cells
Release of mitochondrial AST from alcohol-induced mitochondrial injury
questions.e: The AST:ALT ratio of 2:1 or more comes from relative pyridoxal-5-phosphate deficiency (ALT needs more) plus mitochondrial AST release from alcohol-damaged mitochondria.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the stem to the underlying biology.
Ratio about **2.7**; B6 already accounted for, so think about **where AST lives**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Release of mitochondrial AST from alcohol-induced mitochondrial injury.

elim: Would show raised troponin; the source here is the liver.
Would give anaemia with a raised LDH, not a 2:1 ratio pattern.
Bile duct injury raises ALP and GGT, not AST.
Transaminases are not cleared by the kidneys in a way that explains this.

steps.x: **E. Release of mitochondrial AST from alcohol-induced mitochondrial injury.** High AST:ALT = low B6 (less ALT) + mitochondrial AST release.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man who drinks 3 litres of strong cider a day is admitted with alcoholic hepatitis. He eats a normal amount but has chronic diarrhoea. His red cell transketolase activity is low. The student asks why heavy drinkers become thiamine deficient even when they eat.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his thiamine deficiency?
o: Alcohol impairs thiamine absorption and depletes hepatic stores
Increased thiamine destruction by stomach acid
Thiamine is bound and inactivated by bilirubin
questions.e: Alcohol impairs gut absorption of thiamine and depletes the liver's thiamine stores, so drinkers become deficient even with an adequate intake.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the stem to the underlying biology.

clues: 3 litres of strong cider a day
red cell transketolase activity is low
steps.x: Deficient **despite eating**: alcohol must affect absorption and storage.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Alcohol impairs thiamine absorption and depletes hepatic stores.

elim: He is not on diuretics; this is not the main mechanism.
Not a recognised mechanism.
Causes vitamin B12, not thiamine, deficiency.
Not a recognised mechanism.

steps.x: **A. Alcohol impairs thiamine absorption and depletes hepatic stores.** Alcohol cuts thiamine absorption and hepatic stores.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man with alcoholic hepatitis develops nystagmus, an unsteady gait and confusion. A student asks why lack of one vitamin can damage the brain so quickly, especially in areas with high energy use such as the mammillary bodies.
questions.q: Which is the most likely role of the deficient vitamin?
questions.e: Thiamine is an essential cofactor for cerebral glucose metabolism (pyruvate dehydrogenase, transketolase); deficiency, worse if glucose is given without thiamine, precipitates Wernicke's.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the stem to the underlying biology.

clues: nystagmus, an unsteady gait and confusion
steps.x: **Wernicke's** triad; which vitamin powers brain energy metabolism?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Cofactor for cerebral glucose metabolism.

elim: Vitamin C; deficiency causes scurvy.
Vitamin B12; causes subacute combined degeneration.
Vitamin A; deficiency causes night blindness.
Vitamin D.

steps.x: **A. Cofactor for cerebral glucose metabolism.** Thiamine: cofactor for cerebral glucose metabolism.

questions.stem: A 53 year old woman is admitted with alcoholic hepatitis.
